text: To get a teardown/recreate race, force the activity to be destroyed instead of relying on timing. First check the activity's configChanges in the manifest. If it declares none, rotating to landscape or turning on dark mode destroys and recreates the activity. That also tears down the preview surface and the native engine. This is faster and more reliable than timing a backgrounding against async w

Before you write a real-tap repro, run a direct engine-call replay: destroy the player, sleep about 500 ms, create the player again if needed, then make a call that comes after the teardown. For a crash in a per-clip engine query, query a clip id the new engine does not have. These replays reached the field frames in about 1–2 minutes, and in one case hit every field frame.

Fire triggers and judge checkpoints from engine log lines, not from fixed delays or UI events. Arm the replay on a when_log line, for example when a converted clip reaches the engine or when the engine destructor message prints. Then fire the lifecycle action (home, rotate) right away, or tap the next screen that still calls the engine. A fixed delay only hits some of the time.

Never guess which UI action sends an engine message, and never guess where a control is. Find in the code which confirmed UI action actually sends the expected engine message, and script exactly that action. Opening and leaving a tool is often not enough, because the app may send the message only after an edit is confirmed. Read the real control bounds from a uiautomator dump or a screen dump.

Control the project/draft state and the test content, and write every recipe for the draft it will actually start from. First check that the draft meets the field's preconditions, such as the number of clips on the target layer and special items like freezes. The default lab-phone draft has a single long clip, so split and trim checkpoints can never fire from it.

If two or three recipes in a row miss the first checkpoint, replay one specific field instance in full: its device, its action sequence and its real gaps between taps. On low-end devices, slow the phone down. In one job this reproduced the crash on the first try after step-by-step recipes kept missing.

An ANR in the lab is not a repro unless its main-thread frames match the field. The same function can be reached by other routes (draft open, back from a tool screen) and give a KeyEvent ANR with a different stack. Never use a hook that fabricates the hang itself: it gives false hits that do not match the field.

When the ANR trigger is a heavy edit reload, try undo/redo early. Tapping the edit's apply button three times did not produce a main-thread ANR. Undo/redo of the same edit did on the first try, because it replays the full engine reload back-to-back while the UI posts a blocking query. The undo-button step (ve_btn_undo) once failed with 'not found' on both the phone and the emulator, so check that

To make an engine-thread race or a lock-contention ANR fire, start playback just before the edit tap. The render loop then holds the GL context or lease when the edit message arrives. With the player paused, the lease is taken at once and the stall never shows.

Make one attempt per app process, and make sure the old process is really gone. Start every repro cycle from a fresh process with exactly the activity stack you intend. Do not call open_draft or the open-editor/slideshow step on top of a live child screen, and do not call it again inside a recipe: the stack it leaves will not reach the teardown checkpoint. Each reopen also kills the app.

Trust the physical phone lane, and plan for it to supply all the clean runs you need on its own. The emulator lane is unreliable: it once did not boot within 360 s and was skipped, and the APK install once failed on the first try. Recipes recorded on the phone failed every time on the emulator with 'live replay: not found' for a back-button content-desc. The emulator is also offline, so catalog do

Lab fixture projects exist only on the device where they were built, and the device that hit the crash is not always one of the current lanes. If ed.open_fixture names an id that is missing on a lane, the run fails about 8 s in, still on MainActivity. Before writing a recipe that uses a fixture, check that the fixture exists on every target serial (the phone and emulator-5554).

Treat these harness outputs as background noise, not as a crash, repro or fix-regression signal: (1) the UNDO_WITHOUT_EDITS note ('Undo became enabled with no edits'), which appears on nearly every scenario run, including runs with no edits, engine replays and the real-taps replay, has no engine aborts and does not fail the run; (2) repeated 'FD from fork' messages.

A verify recipe must replay exactly the path that crashed. Some recipes randomize per seed (leave by back key or tap, drag direction, timing), so one crashing seed does not prove the recipe is reliable. Pin it to the crashing path. A crash found by a live agent can be registered as a recipe that keeps only the navigation taps and drops the steps that actually triggered it, so check that the trigge

Plan for the real-taps replay to run with lab shortcuts off (ZESTY_LAB=0, --record). Stop the recipe at the crash moment, and make every step before it work with real taps. Steps after the trigger that need lab shortcuts cause automation errors: they made the first verify inconclusive, and the screen-recorded repro video failed 3 times. The replay also cannot reach the editor unless the navigation

Judge verify runs strictly. A clean run counts only if it reached every field crash/trigger checkpoint and the engine log was actually captured. Some runs return no engine MsgLooper lines and cannot be judged, so check for those lines on both the phone and emulator lanes. A clean engine replay plus clean real-tap runs is still unverified if the real-tap runs never reached the crash moment.

Patches (fixes and repro hooks) must apply to and compile against what the lab actually builds. Lab builds swap in the field-commit versions of the files on the crash stack. So write every diff with exact line context: against the field-commit version for crash-stack files, and against the current working tree for all other files. Never write a diff from code remembered from earlier attempts.

The harness reuses a cached APK whenever the code state hash matches, so install takes about 20 s instead of a full compile. Keep the set of files pinned to the field commit stable between attempts so later runs hit the cache.

Budget lab time realistically. A verify round takes about 40–45 minutes: about 1.5 minutes for the incremental arm64 build, then 2 + 6 scenario runs that each stop at about 300 s (4–5 minutes per run). A real-tap verify run takes about 3 minutes. Each natural focus run with a long clip took about 225 s, so 3 repeats cost about 11 minutes. The emulator lane takes about 40 s to boot, plus a test-dra

If the fixture builder fails twice with the same automation error (for example, a bottom bar item it cannot reach), retrying it unchanged will not help. Change how it reaches that tool (scroll the bar, or target the item by its content description), or move on to recipes that set up the project themselves.

The root-cause self-check rejects claims that hold for only one event: timings, error order, or errors missing from other events. Such claims cost two redo rounds of about 2 minutes each. Before submitting, check that every timing, error and step in the trigger is present in every event, and keep single-event claims out of the main story.

For use-after-teardown or null-object crashes, fix it once at the shared getter, or make the owner live for the whole process. This matters most when the null owner is reached from many JNI entry points. A guard that only makes the faulting function return a default value (0, empty, null, or a thrown exception) often just moves the crash. A native guard that throws inside a looper message is espec

For an out-of-range index crash, unlike use-after-teardown crashes, a bounds guard at the crash site is the right fix. Reject exactly the out-of-range inputs: an invalid outer index, and an inner index past the container size. This passed the critic and code review on the first round. The reviewer checks that the guard covers every index the loop reads, so state that coverage in the fix.

For an ANR where the main thread sits in a blocking engine Get/GetResult call, do not only harden the wait. First look for a Java/Kotlin caller that polls the engine in a loop on the main thread with no exit condition or timeout. Hardening only the engine promise path failed the lab twice, because that loop kept issuing new blocking calls. The proposer gate also rejects any diff that only adds a t

A focused run (set by the flag file) runs only the registered ladder recipes. It has no engine replay, live agent or repro author to fall back on. Use it only when the registered recipe is known to reach its trigger. If the single registered step misses, clear the flag so the other repro paths can try, or register a stronger hook-based step. Do not rerun the same recipe.

For ANRs caused by slow work blocking the main thread, natural runs with the lab boost (watchdog 0 ms, CPU load x6) can still pass cleanly every time. If the first natural ladder step shows anrsan=0 in every run, move straight to the hook-assisted runs (the debug.zesty.hook.* sysprops that slow down or empty the suspect path), because those are what confirmed the trigger.

Check the scenario's own progress counters (for example 'speed apply 3/5') before you trust a PASS. If the trigger action ran on only some of its planned iterations, the run did not fully exercise the race, so fix the scenario's UI driving before adding more repeats.
